anomaly_def.Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: A static mismatch between table structures, indexes, partitions, and the workload’s access predicates that forces the optimizer onto wide scans, non-covering index probes, or hot-page insert patterns.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly: Intensive competition among sessions for buffer-pool pages, page pins, and latches that serialises access, causes CPU spin or waits, and throttles throughput even when higher-level locks are free.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly: Exhaustion of kernel-enforced resources—file descriptors, shared-memory segments, semaphores, thread slots, AIO contexts, cgroup quotas—preventing the database from allocating memory, buffers, or worker processes.

When all three root causes coexist, the workload exhibits extreme and erratic latency, bursty throughput, and frequent transient errors. Full-table scans and non-selective index access flood the limited buffer cache, evicting useful pages and triggering constant physical I/O. The undersized or starved buffer pool amplifies buffer-busy waits and page-latch contention as hot root pages, sequence blocks, or last pages of append-only tables are thrashed by concurrent sessions. Simultaneously, the operating system intermittently refuses additional shared-memory allocations, file opens, or thread spawns, leading to sudden query failures, stalled background writers, or disabled parallel plans. Monitoring views show a mix of high logical I/O, spikes in BUFFER_BUSY/LATCH_* waits, and kernel-level "Too many open files", "ENOMEM", or "semget failed" messages, making it difficult to attribute the slowdown to a single layer.

Causally, the poor schema and index design enlarges the I/O footprint and concentrates activity on a small set of pages. This load magnifies buffer-pool pressure; because OS-level limits cap the cache size or the number of shared-memory segments, the engine cannot keep enough pages resident, leading to relentless eviction and reload cycles. Each reload requires latches and I/O slots, increasing contention inside the buffer manager. As contention lengthens critical-section hold times, latch spin and sleep escalate CPU consumption, while OS resource denials further reduce available worker threads or AIO descriptors, stretching I/O completion times and checkpoint flushes. The three issues thus form a reinforcing loop: sub-optimal data access inflates buffer demand, restricted OS resources prevent the cache or process pool from scaling, and the overstressed buffer manager becomes a hotspot, collectively degrading both transactional and analytical workloads.

entry.official_definition: Specifies the number of TCP keepalive messages that can be lost before the server connection to the client is considered dead.
entry.trigger_condition: The number of lost TCP keepalive probes reaches tcp_keepalives_count on systems supporting TCP_KEEPCNT.
entry.workload_impact: The server can consider the client connection dead after the configured keepalive failure threshold.
entry.default_behavior: Default value is 0, selecting the operating system default.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when connection establishment, authentication exchange, or session activity does not progress within the allowed time budget.
entry.solution_guidance: Check connection lifecycle, client responsiveness, authentication latency, idle-session handling, and whether connection pools are holding stale sessions.
